doc.title: Tom Lellis interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, July 31, 2007

title: Nancy Wilson recording and studying singers
summary: Rowe plays a Nancy Wilson record; Lellis describes studying singers closely, Carmen McRae last, then turning to instrumentalists at about 24.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Well I promised I would play a couple of things for you. Let me see if I can make this happen here.
Yeah. I’m just curious if you recall this particular record as a singer. It’s not the ones I was looking for. Here’s one I was looking for.

“Happy Talk.” Sure. She’s killing, Nancy. And “Never Will I Marry” oh my, my. No, Nancy’s beautiful. You know I studied all this. I didn’t mention Nancy and I should have. I studied as many of the good singers as I could, I mean laying down on the floor in front of the speakers just studying them. And I went through all of them and the last one was Carmen McRae, who I’m born on Carmen’s birthday and I didn’t even know that, and I just loved the way she could go from soft and tender to hard and edgy and nasty almost. And she is a great interpreter. And then I stopped, at about 24, when I started playing piano, I stopped listening to singers for influence. I went to the instrumentalists. And I think it’s, with all the influence that I got from these wonderful singers, then I went to the instrumentalists who were playing all these different linear approaches. And that’s how I hoped I would develop into something slightly different than my predecessors. And I don’t know if I have or not but I know that the study of music has helped me to go to places that some, I feel a lot of singers, haven’t gone, at least on that path. But she is so good.
